Ensuring the integrity of our export controls is central to advancing America’s national security and our long-term economic prosperity, including by preventing China – our only near-peer competitor – from obtaining advanced U.S. technologies with military applications, such as cutting-edge artificial intelligence (AI) chips. Our export control regime must be able to identify and curtail entities actively seeking to evade those controls.

Reports indicate that Megaspeed operates AI data centers in Southeast Asia, potentially with Nvidia Blackwell processors, and may have used them to provide Chinese clients with remote cloud computing power from restricted U.S. hardware. As of October 29, 2026, Nvidia continued to list Megaspeed on its website as a cloud partner. This highlights another gap in current U.S. export control regulations, since the administration has not imposed restrictions to prevent companies headquartered in countries outside of China, like Megaspeed, from providing Chinese clients remote access to export-controlled chips.

Reports indicate that Megaspeed operated as a middle man, using Aivres – a U.S.-registered subsidiary of Chinese technology giant Inspur, on which the United States imposed sanctions for supporting China’s military – to source restricted hardware, such as advanced Nvidia AI chips. Aivres was able to purchase this hardware (1) because Aivres was not subject to the sanctions imposed on its parent company Inspur; (2) because the Department of Commerce has rolled back steps that restrict the subsidiaries of Chinese-headquartered firms from buying export-controlled AI chips from U.S. firms; and (3) because the Department of Commerce halted enforcement of licensing requirements for Chinese-headquartered subsidiaries in Malaysia from May 2025, creating more loopholes that have enabled the illicit diversion of sensitive U.S. technology. Aivres thus continued purchasing advanced Nvidia chips, which a Malaysia-based Megaspeed subsidiary then bought. BIS officials who visited Megaspeed’s Malaysia data center suspected that Megaspeed may have sent some of these chips to China. Meanwhile, Aivres currently advertises access to Nvidia’s most advanced and recently released Vera Rubin chips.
